stem: Mean arterial pressure is calculated by adding what fraction of the pulse pressure to the diastolic pressure?

options.label: A
options.misconception: Systolic pressure is being overweighted relative to diastolic.
options.explanation: Adding two-thirds of the pulse pressure overweights systole; the correct weighting is one-third above diastolic.

options.label: B
options.misconception: The entire systolic-diastolic difference is being added to diastolic.
options.explanation: Adding the full pulse pressure would approximate systolic pressure, not the time-averaged mean.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero — MAP equals diastolic pressure alone
options.misconception: The contribution of systolic pressure during systole is being ignored entirely.
options.explanation: Diastolic pressure alone ignores systolic flow during systole; one-third of the pulse pressure must be added.

options.label: D
options.misconception: The arithmetic midpoint of systolic and diastolic is being used instead of the time-weighted mean.
options.explanation: Diastole lasts longer than systole, so the mean is weighted toward diastolic pressure; one-half would equal the simple midpoint, not MAP.

options.label: E
options.misconception: None; MAP equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure.
options.explanation: Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the difference between systolic and diastolic pressures.

context: Learning objective: state the MAP formula. Mean arterial pressure equals diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic).
